title: Hard to be born human (179–182)
hook: hard is it to be born human, hard the life of mortals, hard to hear the true teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, candimā: the careless one who turns earnest and gives light. Your line was the moon comes out. What did you begin again? Day one hundred ninety-three, and chapter fourteen begins: the Buddha.

It's a Tuesday. You woke up, found the coffee, checked the weather, and went through the usual list of complaints. Nothing special happened. And yet: you woke up. You have a mind that can wonder about its own life. You're listening to words that were first spoken twenty-five centuries ago and still reached you. None of that feels rare, because it happens every day. Chapter fourteen of the Dhammapada is about the Buddha, and in the middle of it sits one verse that takes this perfectly ordinary Tuesday and turns it over to show the price tag. Today: hard to be born human.
screen: `AN ORDINARY TUESDAY.` → `YOU WOKE UP.` → `THE PRICE TAG ON A DAY.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens by praising the Awakened One as trackless: no desire can lead him anywhere, so there's no trail to follow him by. Verse one eighty-one even says the gods envy those who are awake. Then verse one eighty-two, in Max Müller's words: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals, difficult is the hearing of the True Law, difficult is the birth of the Awakened." In Pali, each line begins with the same word, kiccha: hard, difficult, rare. Hard to be born human. Hard to live as a mortal. Hard to hear the true teaching. Hard for a Buddha to appear at all. Four rarities stacked on top of each other, and you're standing on all four. The Buddha gave a famous picture of how rare. In the Samyutta Nikaya, he asks the monks to imagine a yoke with a single hole, tossed on the ocean and blown about by the winds. Once every hundred years, a blind turtle rises to the surface. What are the chances the turtle puts its head through that hole? That, he says, is how rare it is for a being who has fallen into the lower realms to come back to a human birth. You don't have to hold the Buddhist view of many lives to feel what this verse is doing. It takes the thing you complain about every morning and shows you it's a winning ticket. Buddhists hear it as urgency, not guilt: this life, with a mind that can learn and a teaching within reach, is the rare chance. The list of complaints can stay; it just doesn't get the whole day.
screen: `THE TRACKLESS ONE.` · `KICCHA — HARD, RARE.` · `A BLIND TURTLE AND A YOKE.` · `A WINNING TICKET, NOT GUILT.` · then, large: `THIS LIFE IS RARE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let today be completely ordinary. Now go through it slowly. You're breathing: rare. You can hear: rare. There's someone, somewhere, you love or who loves you: rare. There's food in your day, a roof, a moment to sit: not everyone has these. You've heard a teaching, and you're thinking about it: rare. Don't force gratitude. Just let each ordinary thing be seen once, the way you'd look again at something you almost threw away. Then rest in this one rare breath. The bell holds the time.
Kiccha. Hard, difficult, rare: verse one eighty-two says rare is human birth, rare a mortal life, rare the hearing of the teaching, rare the arising of a Buddha.
Your line: this life is rare. Today, pick one ordinary hour and treat it like the winning ticket it is. Day one hundred ninety-three.

screen: `DAY 193 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TEACHING OF ALL BUDDHAS.`

howItsDone: Many Buddhist traditions, Theravada and Tibetan alike, begin practice by reflecting on the preciousness and rarity of a human life, often using the Buddha's image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

pairs: a blind turtle and a yoke
the Buddha, led by no desire
even the gods envy the awake

myth: human birth, a mortal life, hearing the true teaching, and a Buddha arising.
the turtle rises to the surface once a year
once every hundred years, and the yoke has only one hole.
Buddhists hear this verse mainly as a reason for guilt
they hear urgency: a rare chance, not a debt.

fork.setup: a blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years. a yoke with one hole drifts on the whole ocean. what is the Buddha comparing it to?
options: the chance of being born human.
the chance of meeting a friend.
fork.reveal: that's how rare the tradition says a human birth is: so rare that an ordinary Tuesday is a winning ticket.

original.note: Pali: a human being — in verse 182, gaining a human birth is kiccha, hard.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is hard.
what it means: life is rare: a human birth, a mind that can learn and a teaching in reach are a precious chance.
what a scholar hears: each line of verse 182 opens with kiccha, and the blind-turtle simile in the Samyutta Nikaya sizes the rarity.

notes: Blind turtle simile: SN 56.47 (yoke with one hole, turtle surfacing once every hundred years); in the sutta it concerns a fool reborn in lower realms regaining human birth; simplified here. Confirm.
Pali 'kiccho manussapaṭilābho, kicchaṃ maccāna jīvitaṃ, kicchaṃ saddhammassavanaṃ, kiccho buddhānaṃ uppādo'; confirm.
'You don't have to hold the Buddhist view of many lives to feel what this verse is doing' written for mixed listeners; confirm tone.
Müller quotations checked against the Project Gutenberg text of SBE vol. 10 (ebook #2017); confirm against the 1881 printing.

Audit 2026-09-30: the blind-turtle simile now says what SN 56.47 actually compares (a being in the lower realms regaining human birth), and the closing imperative 'Don't spend it all on the list of complaints' was softened so it no longer lectures the listener.
